column14: notes
Sinatra/Andy Williams/soundtrack-adjacent adult pop. Declines but real: 'Sound of Music' OST was #1 album of 1966-68.
Herb Alpert/Tijuana Brass instrumental pop. Mid-decade bump: 4 TJB albums in Billboard Top 10 simultaneously, 1966.
Teen idols (Fabian, Bobby Vee, Lesley Gore). Collapses fast post-1964 as British Invasion displaces the format.
Broader UK pop beyond Merseybeat proper - Kinks, Herman's Hermits, Dave Clark Five, Petula Clark, Peter & Gordon.
Retrospective label for mid-60s bright-harmony pop (Association, 5th Dimension precursors). Real but never a trade category.
Retrospective label (Left Banke, Zombies orchestral material). Small, real, peaks 1967.
1910 Fruitgum Co, Ohio Express (1968); Archies 'Sugar Sugar' was best-selling single of 1969.
Chuck Berry/Little Richard/early Elvis style. Declining tag, not a late-decade catch-all - superseded by named subgenres below.
Merseybeat proper: Beatles + Liverpool peers. Beatles held Billboard Hot 100 top 5 simultaneously, April 4 1964.
Stones/Yardbirds/Animals/Mayall's Bluesbreakers/Cream. Grows through decade as UK blues-rock scene matures.
Breaks nationally with the Byrds' 'Mr. Tambourine Man' and Dylan going electric, 1965.
Late-decade Gram Parsons direction - Byrds' 'Sweetheart of the Rodeo' (1968), Dylan's 'Nashville Skyline' (1969).
Beach Boys/Jan & Dean/Dick Dale. Peaks 1963, dented hard by the British Invasion from 1964.
Mid-60s British-Invasion-inspired US garage boom - '96 Tears', Nuggets-era bands. Fades as scene diffuses into psych, 1968+.
Velvet Underground (1967), Stooges/MC5 forming late 60s. Not a commercial chart force in this decade.
Heavier psych variant (Hendrix, Cream). Overlaps PsychedelicRock; kept small and parallel to it.
Peaks 1967 - Sgt. Pepper, Are You Experienced, Surrealistic Pillow, Summer of Love. Diffuses into other rock forms by 1969.
British art-rock transition, Moody Blues/Procol Harum 1967-68; true commercial prog is 1969-71 (King Crimson, Oct 1969).
American wing of the blues-rock boom - Butterfield Blues Band, Canned Heat. Smaller than the British scene this decade.
Cream/Who power, Steppenwolf, Blue Cheer edge. Full commercial emergence is 1970 (Zeppelin II, Sabbath), still building here.
Iron Butterfly, Blue Cheer, Sabbath-edges. 'In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida' was a top seller of 1969 despite the genre staying niche.
Platters/Drifters style vocal harmony. Largely a 1950s style with an early-60s tail; gone as a chart force by 1963.
Pre-soul rhythm & blues. Gradually cedes ground to Soul as the decade's Black-pop center of gravity shifts.
Otis Redding/Aretha/Sam Cooke/Motown-adjacent. Should be robust and rising mid-to-late decade, not middling.
James Brown's late-60s evolution - 'Cold Sweat' (1967) is the usual root marker. Zero before that.
Steady niche; crossover bump from Edwin Hawkins Singers' 'Oh Happy Day', a #4 Hot 100 hit in 1969.
Nashville sound, Patsy Cline. Comparatively stable all decade - no mid-decade national mega-share explosion.
Kingston Trio/early Dylan collegiate folk revival. Declines as Folk Rock and Contemporary Folk peel off its audience.
More personal/poetic acoustic folk (Baez, Ochs, Tim Hardin) - bridge between Folk and Singer-Songwriter.
Emerging tendency - Cohen, early Joni Mitchell/Van Morrison/James Taylor. Mainstream breakthrough is 1970-71, still small here.
Dave Brubeck/Miles Davis crossover. Steady gradual decline in pop-chart share as rock's share grows.
Straight electric/acoustic blues - B.B. King, Muddy Waters, John Lee Hooker. Small steady niche throughout.
Crossover classical/novelty. Small bump 1968 from 'Switched-On Bach' (Wendy Carlos), a genuine crossover hit.
Jazz Samba (1962) through Getz/Gilberto (1964, Grammy Album of the Year 1965). Craze fades by 1966.
NYC Latin-soul fusion - Joe Cuba, Pete Rodriguez. Regional, peaks ~1966-68, fades as salsa emerges.
Sir Douglas Quintet and similar. Small steady regional presence throughout.
Mainstream Latin-flavored pop crossover. Small, steady presence.
Jamaican ska; minimal US national chart share this decade. Desmond Dekker's 'Israelites' (1969) is the era's real US crossover.
Jamaican transitional style 1966-68, between ska and reggae. Essentially no US national chart share.
Term coined ~1968 (Toots and the Maytals). US mainstream reggae breakthrough is 1970s, not this decade.
Novelty/comedy records - Allan Sherman, Ray Stevens. Small steady chart presence throughout.
Disney and kiddie-market novelty records. Small steady niche.
